sections.h2: Which Madison County offices handle a property tax bill?
sections.html:
Two offices in the Government Complex at 91 Albany Avenue in Danielsville split the work. Property Valuation, which serves the Board of Assessors, sets the value of your land and house. The Tax Commissioner bills, collects and records payment.

Send questions to the right desk and the answer comes faster. A wrong acreage, a missing exemption or a disagreement over value goes to Property Valuation. A balance, a payment method or a receipt goes to the Tax Commissioner. The county also lists a parcel search through qPublic, which shows ownership and value for each Madison County tract.

Madison County tax offices in Danielsville (source: Madison County government website)

The Tax Commissioner's office keeps a drop box behind the government complex for payments left outside business hours. It is the only place in the county that bills and collects property, mobile home and timber tax.

sections.h2: What should a Madison County seller know about the county itself?
sections.html:
Madison County is a rural, mostly residential county just north and east of Athens. The county's own history page says it was the 38th county formed in Georgia, created in 1811 from pieces of Clarke, Elbert, Franklin, Jackson and Oglethorpe counties, and named for President James Madison. Danielsville is the seat, and the other five municipalities are Carlton, Colbert, Comer, Hull and Ila.

Farming still shapes the local economy. The county reports that about 23 percent of its land is prime agricultural land and that poultry and egg production matter most. Watson Mill Bridge State Park, shared with Oglethorpe County, holds the longest covered bridge in Georgia, and the 1901 county courthouse in Danielsville is on the National Register of Historic Places.

  • Census estimate for July 2025: 32,919 residents, up 9.3 percent from the April 2020 base of 30,116.
  • Land area of 282.32 square miles and 106.7 people per square mile in 2020.
  • Owner-occupied rate of 76.9 percent across 11,242 households.
  • Median owner-occupied value of $219,700 and median gross rent of $972 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median household income of $61,963 and a mean commute of 29.5 minutes.
  • 130 building permits issued in 2025.

Those figures come from Census QuickFacts. A commute near half an hour reflects how many residents drive to jobs in Athens, Commerce and Elberton.

sections.h2: How does Madison County arrive at the value of a house?
sections.html:
The assessors estimate fair market value as of January 1 and tax 40 percent of it. The county's Property Valuation page says the office uses three approaches: comparable sales, replacement cost less depreciation plus land value, and income capitalization for investment property.

An assessment notice normally goes out between April and May. It is not a bill. It shows the appraised value that the next bill will be built on, so a seller who plans to list in spring should read it the day it arrives.

Returns run on a fixed window. Georgia owners file between January 1 and April 1, and Madison County takes them at Property Valuation. After the first return, the law renews it each year at the last final value. A new return is needed only when you add property, build, or want to declare a different value.

  • A site visit by a field appraiser means measuring structures and taking photographs. Staff carry photo identification and drive marked county vehicles.
  • Conservation use and other specialized assessments must be applied for by April 1 to count for that tax year.
  • The Board of Assessors accepts only a U.S. Postal Service postmark as proof of timing for returns, homestead applications and appeals.

sections.h2: When are Madison County property taxes billed and due?
sections.html:
Real and personal property bills are generally mailed in September and carry a normal due date of December 20. The Tax Commissioner accepts partial payments, so a seller who cannot clear the whole bill can still reduce it before closing.

Mobile homes run on their own calendar. Their bills are generally mailed in late January and are due April 1. A mobile home with a homestead exemption does not get that early bill, and its tax appears on the year-end property bill instead.

State guidance adds one more rule that matters to anyone selling late in the year. A taxpayer is given 60 days from the postmark of the bill before interest accrues, though the county's official due date on the bill is the one to follow. Timber works differently, because standing timber is assessed once, when it is sold or harvested, at full fair market value, and that tax is paid to the Tax Commissioner of the county where the trees grew.

Ask the Tax Commissioner for a written payoff on the parcel before you sign a sale contract. That number, not a guess from last year's bill, is what a closing attorney will want.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Madison County assessment?
sections.html:
You have 45 days from the date printed on the assessment notice, and the appeal must be postmarked by the U.S. Postal Service within that window. Madison County states in plain terms that it does not accept appeals by fax, email or any other electronic route.

The county's published steps are short. Write a letter that names the parcel number, gives the reason and includes a phone number. Staff review it and may call to set up an appointment. If the assessors agree, you are notified. If they do not, the file moves automatically to the Board of Equalization, or to arbitration if you asked for that in your first letter.

  • Valid grounds are value, taxability and equalization. The amount of tax is not a valid reason.
  • The Board of Equalization is chosen by the grand jury and costs nothing to use.
  • Arbitration means each side picks and pays its own arbitrator and splits the cost of a third.
  • A Superior Court appeal carries a $25 filing fee, according to the county.
  • After a Board of Equalization or court decision, the assessors cannot change the result for two years without a site inspection or a new return.

Sale prices and photographs of similar homes that sold recently are the evidence the county invites. Miss the window and the right to appeal that year is forfeited.

sections.h2: Which homestead exemptions does Madison County offer?
sections.html:
Homestead applications are taken at Property Valuation between January 1 and April 1, and you must own and live in the home on January 1 of that year. File after April 1 and the exemption starts the following year.

The county's list uses short codes. S1 is the standard owner-occupied residence exemption. S3 and L3 are for owners 62 or older with income under $10,000 for the applicant and spouse, not counting Social Security and retirement. L4 applies at 65 and L5 at 70, with no income test. S5 covers a 100 percent disabled veteran or the unremarried surviving spouse. SG covers the unremarried surviving spouse of a firefighter or peace officer killed in the line of duty, and SS covers the unremarried surviving spouse of a service member killed in action.

The City of Colbert offers its own homestead exemption for homes inside the city limits, and the county tells owners to contact Colbert directly. Ask the clerk of any other Madison County town whether it levies a separate city tax before you assume a single county bill covers everything.

A buyer who plans to live in the house has to file again in their own name, because the seller's exemption does not carry to the new owner.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax bill when I sell a Madison County house?
sections.html:
Property tax follows the owner of record on January 1, so a house sold in the summer can still produce a bill in your name that fall. Your sale contract decides who reimburses whom, and the closing statement is where it gets settled.

Georgia also charges a real estate transfer tax when a deed is recorded. The Department of Revenue prints the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100, and says the seller is liable unless the contract moves it to the buyer. Questions about taxability go to the Clerk of Superior Court.

If your land was ever sold at a Madison County delinquent tax sale, the Tax Commissioner publishes an excess funds list and an application for anyone owed money after that sale. Heirs and former owners should check it.

  • Get the payoff from the Tax Commissioner before closing.
  • Check that the homestead exemption comes off after the sale.
  • Report address changes in writing so bills reach you.

faqs.q: When are Madison County, GA property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real and personal property bills usually go out in September and have a normal due date of December 20, while mobile home taxes are due April 1. The date printed on your bill controls, so confirm it with the Tax Commissioner at 706-795-6385.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Madison County value by email?
faqs.a: No. The Board of Assessors accepts appeals only with a U.S. Postal Service postmark inside 45 days of the notice date, and it refuses fax and email. Write a letter with the parcel number, your reason and a phone number.

faqs.q: Who sets my Madison County property value?
faqs.a: The Board of Assessors, working through the Property Valuation office, sets the value. The Tax Commissioner does not report to the assessors and only collects what the digest produces.

faqs.q: Do I have to reapply for homestead exemption every year?
faqs.a: Madison County's page describes a one-time filing window of January 1 to April 1 for the year you first claim it. A new owner files in their own name, and an application made after April 1 starts the next tax year. Ask Property Valuation whether anything must be refiled.

faqs.q: Does Madison County take partial property tax payments?
faqs.a: Yes. The Tax Commissioner's office states that partial payments on property taxes are accepted. Ask for a payoff in writing so the balance is clear before you close.
